title: Philosophy of religion
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Examine the main questions of the philosophy of religion fairly, drawing on several traditions: the concept of God and the divine attributes, cosmological, design, fine-tuning and ontological arguments, the principle of sufficient reason, religious experience, the logical and evidential problems of evil, miracles, faith and reason, religious diversity, and non-theistic and naturalistic views.
primary_reading: Introduction to Philosophy: Philosophy of Religion (Rebus Community, free)

weeks.1: What the philosophy of religion asks
weeks.2: The concept of God: omnipotence, omniscience and goodness
weeks.3: Cosmological arguments: the kalam and contingency arguments
weeks.7: Ontological arguments: Anselm, Descartes and the modal version
weeks.9: The logical problem of evil and the free will defense
weeks.10: The evidential problem of evil and skeptical theism

blocks.deliverable: Explain the paradox of the stone and two replies.
Reconstruct the contingency argument and its key premise.
Evaluate the fine-tuning argument and the multiverse reply.
Week 7 midterm; reconstruct a modal ontological argument.
Reconstruct the evidential argument from evil and one reply.
Write a balanced essay on one argument.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Balanced dialogue: write a 2,500-word dialogue in which a theist, an atheist and an agnostic examine one argument (cosmological, fine-tuning, ontological or the problem of evil), each giving the strongest version of their view and replying to the others, followed by a one-page assessment of which considerations carry the most weight and why.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
